newsitem.title: USA: Fund investors fret about stock market drop.
newsitem.headline: Fund investors fret about stock market drop.

text.p: A recent Money magazine article pointed out that one-third of the $1.76 trillion currently invested in stock funds entered the market during just the past four years. Moreover, one in five fund shareholders has opened his or her first fund account during the past two years.

Most of that new money has yet to witness a serious decline in share prices. In fact, the stock market hasn't suffered a genuine correction (generally defined as a 10 percent to 20 percent drop) -- let alone a bear market (20 percent or greater drop) -- since 1990.
But count on this: The current bull market will end sooner or later.

When it does, many fund investors will face the first test of their investment careers -- a trial by fire of sorts. Seasoned investors know that success depends most of all upon how you behave when the stock market is falling apart.
When that occurs, you have three alternatives.

-- Abandon stocks altogether. Trouble is, this decision carries its own risk. Often, the stock market's biggest gains occur in short, powerful bursts, and those gains tend to come when people least expect them. A decision to sidestep the stock market's risks even for a few weeks could derail your long-term plans.

-- Stick with stocks and ride out the storm. How long will it last? No one knows, but history suggests that the answer isn't important for truly long-term investors. Stocks' worst-ever return over any five-year period since 1950 has been a 4.2 percent annual loss according to a study by L/G Research. Over 10 years, the worst-ever return has been a 0.5 percent annual gain.

-- Buy more. Investors who have the courage to add more money to stocks or stock funds when their prices decline probably will accrue the best returns over long periods. It's a bad idea to invest the money you were saving to make a down payment on your first home or pay for John Jr.'s freshman year at Cal Tech. But if you're stashing part of your paycheck in a retirement account every couple of weeks, it makes sense to keep using the money to buy stocks when they're cheap. The same goes for investors who are saving on their own in an IRA or elsewhere.

But which stocks or funds should you buy when the market skids? It almost doesn't matter, as long as you are diversified reasonably well. The purpose of investing when stock prices decline is to share in the market's long-term gains, not to pick the hottest fund of the coming year.

An index fund such as Vanguard Index Trust Total Stock Market (800-662-7447; $3,000 minimum investment; no load) will do the trick. The fund attempts to track the return of the Wilshire 5000, one of the broadest stock market indices. The fund has posted around 45 percent better returns than its typical competitor during the past three years, with about 20 percent less risk.

You can tilt the odds of success in your favour by choosing funds that invest in the market's least-loved sectors. For example, many funds that invest in shares of small companies have experienced sharp declines. The Nasdaq Composite Index has declined more than 10 percent from its January peak, and many sectors of the small cap market are hurting far worse.

Thus, investors might want to consider a stake in a small company fund such as Compass Capital Small Cap Growth (888-426-6727; $5,000 minimum; no load). Manager William Wykle looks for firms with earnings and revenue-growth rates of 20 percent or more, low debt and other factors.

If you don't mind some rough sailing, consider a stake in a fund that specialises in the battered technology industry. One solid choice: T. Rowe Price Science & Technology (800-638-5660; $2,500 minimum; no load).

Finally, keep an eye on funds that invest in emerging markets in Latin America, Asia and elsewhere. If the U.S. market nosedives, those funds will temporarily plummet as well as jittery investors pull in their horns around the globe. But such a slump could create opportunities to invest in emerging markets at bargain levels.

Consider a fund such as Templeton Developing Markets (800-292-9293; $100 minimum; 5.75 percent load). Manager Mark Mobius has led the fund to a 14.2 percent return during the past five years, versus 11.1 percent for the typical emerging markets fund.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
